'''''Telopea speciosissima''''', commonly known as the '''New South Wales waratah''' or simply '''waratah''', is a large shrub in the plant family [[Proteaceae]]. It is [[Endemism|endemic]] to [[New South Wales]] in [[Australia]]. No [[subspecies]] are recognised; the closely related ''[[Telopea aspera]]'' was classified as a separate species in 1995. ''T. speciosissima'' is a shrub to {{convert|3|or|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide, with dark green leaves. Its several stems arise from a pronounced woody base known as a [[lignotuber]]. The species is well renowned for its striking large red springtime [[inflorescence|inflorescences (flowerheads)]], each including hundreds of individual [[flower]]s. These are visited by the [[eastern pygmy possum|eastern pygmy possum (''Cercartetus nanus'')]], birds such as [[honeyeater|honeyeaters (Meliphagidae)]], and various insects.

The [[floral emblem]] for its home state of [[New South Wales]], ''Telopea speciosissima'' has featured prominently in art, architecture, and advertising, particularly since [[Federation of Australia|Australian federation]]. Commercially grown in several countries as a cut flower, it is also cultivated in home gardens, requiring good drainage yet adequate moisture, but is vulnerable to various [[fungus|fungal disease]]s and pests. A number of [[cultivar]]s with various shades of red, pink and even white flowers are available. [[Horticulture|Horticulturists]] have also developed [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] with ''[[Telopea oreades|T. oreades]]'' and ''[[Telopea mongaensis|T. mongaensis]]'' which are more tolerant of cold, shade, and heavier soils.

== Description ==
[[File:Telopea speciosissima seedpods.jpg|thumb|left|Seed pods containing several beige seeds at bottom|alt=Several open banana-shaped seedpods hang down from an old flower spike. Within them a few beige seeds are still attached.]]
''Telopea speciosissima'', the New South Wales waratah, is a large, erect shrub up to {{convert|3|or|4|m|ft}} in height with one or more stems.<ref name=ANBG/><ref name=NSW>{{cite web|author1=Crisp, Michael D. |author2=Weston, Peter H |title=''Telopea speciosissima'' (Sm.) R.Br.|work=New South Wales Flora Online|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Telopea~speciosissima|access-date=14 February 2010}}</ref> Arising vertically or near vertically from a large woody base, or [[lignotuber]], the stems are little branched. In late spring, there is a spurt of new growth after flowering, with new shoots often arising from old flowerheads.<ref name=Nixon27/><!-- cites both previous sentences --> The dark green leaves are [[Phyllotaxis|alternate]] and usually coarsely toothed, ranging from {{convert|13|to|25|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in length.<ref name=ANBG/> Enveloped in leafy [[bract]]s, the flowerheads develop over the winter and begin to swell in early spring,<ref name=ANBG/><ref name=Nixon23>Nixon, p. 23.</ref> before opening to reveal the striking [[inflorescence]]s. The exact timing varies across New South Wales, but flowering can begin as early as August in the northern parts of its range, and finish in November in the southern, more elevated areas.<ref name=Nixon27>Nixon, p. 27.</ref> Spot flowering may also occur around March in autumn.<ref name=Nixon24>Nixon, p. 24.</ref> Containing up to 250 individual flowers, the domed flowerheads are crimson in colour and measure {{convert|7|–|10|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter. They are cupped in a [[Phyllotaxis|whorl]] of leafy bracts which are {{convert|5|to|7|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long and also red.<ref name=ANBG/><ref name=Nixon27/> Variations are not uncommon; some flowerheads may be more globular or cone-shaped than dome-shaped, and the bracts may be whitish or dark red. The tips of the [[Stigma (botany)|stigmas]] of some inflorescences may be whitish, contrasting with the red colour of the rest of the flowerhead.<ref name=Nixon25>Nixon, p. 25.</ref>

An individual flowerhead reaches full size about two weeks after first emerging from the bracts, and lasts another two weeks before the flowers fade and fall. In the first phase, the individual small flowers, known as [[Internal structure of a flower|florets]], remain unopened—and the flowerhead retains a compact shape—before they mature and split open, revealing the [[stigma (botany)|stigma]], [[Gynoecium#Carpel morphology|style]], and [[Stamen|anther]]. The anther is [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], lacking a filament, and lies next to the stigma at the end of the style. The outermost florets open first, with [[anthesis]] progressing towards the centre of the flowerhead, which becomes darker and more open in appearance, and begins attracting birds and insects. The [[Ovary (plants)|ovary]] lies at the base of the style and atop a stalk known as the [[gynophore]], and it is from here that the seed pods then develop. Meanwhile, a crescent-shaped [[Nectar#Floral nectaries|nectary]] lies at the base of the gynophore.<ref name=Nixon24/><ref name="Willis59">{{cite journal|last=Willis|first=J. L.|year=1959|title=The genus ''Telopea''|journal=Australian Plants|publisher=Surrey Beatty & Sons|location=Chipping Norton, NSW|volume=1|issue=1|pages=7–10}}</ref>

The seed pods grow to {{convert|8|–|15|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=FOA>{{cite web|title=Telopea speciosissima|work=Flora of Australia online|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/abrs/online-resources/flora/stddisplay.xsql?pnid=2471|access-date=16 February 2010|archive-date=4 June 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604124147/http://www.anbg.gov.au/abrs/online-resources/flora/stddisplay.xsql?pnid=2471|url-status=dead}}</ref> As the pods mature, they range from green, to yellow and finally turn russet red-brown. The pods become leathery before splitting open during early winter.<ref name=Nixon24/> The pods contain winged seeds inside.<ref name=ANBG/> In the wild, only two or three seed pods develop per flowerhead, but there may be anywhere from 5 to 50 in cultivated plants.<ref name=Nixon24/>

== Taxonomy ==
[[Image:Embothrium speciosissimum (Sowerby).jpg|thumb|Hand-coloured engraving of ''Telopea speciosissima'' by [[James Sowerby]] from ''A Specimen of the Botany of New Holland''|alt=An old colour drawing of a single red flowerhead on a stem]]
''Telopea speciosissima'', the New South Wales Waratah, was first described by botanist [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in his 1793 book ''[[A Specimen of the Botany of New Holland]]'', from "very fine dried specimens sent by [[John White (surgeon)|Mr. White]]".<ref name="APNI1">{{cite web |url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/name/apni/111597 |title=''Embothrium speciosissimum'' |website=[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI) |publisher=Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, [[Australian Government]] |access-date=15 March 2023}}</ref> He gave the species its original binomial name of ''Embothrium speciosissimum''.<ref name=APNI1/> The [[Specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] is derived from the [[superlative]] of the [[Latin]] word  {{lang|la|specious}} {{gloss|beautiful, handsome}}, hence {{gloss|very-}} or {{gloss|most beautiful}}.<ref name=ANBG>{{cite web |author=Bowden Anne|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/emblems/nsw.emblem.html |title=Floral Emblem of New South Wales |access-date=27 March 2008 |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens}}</ref> ''Embothrium'' had been a [[wastebasket taxon]] at the time, and [[Robert Brown (Scottish botanist from Montrose)|Robert Brown]] suggested the genus ''[[Waratah|Telopea]]'' for it in 1809, which was published in 1810.<ref name="APNI2">{{cite web |url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/name/apni/99835 |title=''Telopea speciosissima'' |website=[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI) |publisher=Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, [[Australian Government]] |access-date=15 March 2023}}</ref> [[Richard Anthony Salisbury|Richard Salisbury]] had published the name ''Hylogyne speciosa'' in 1809, but Brown's name was [[conserved name|nomenclaturally conserved]].<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/><!-- cites para -->

''Telopea speciosissima'' is one of five species from southeastern Australia which make up the genus ''Telopea''. Its closest relative is the very similar Gibraltar Range waratah (''[[Telopea aspera|T. aspera]]'') from northern New South Wales, which was only recognised as a separate species in 1995, having previously been considered an unusual northern population of ''T. speciosissima''.<ref name=FoA>{{cite book|author1=Crisp, Michael D. |author2=Weston, Peter H. |year=1995|chapter=''Telopea''|editor=McCarthy, Patrick|title=Flora of Australia: Volume 16: Eleagnaceae, Proteaceae 1|pages=386–390|publisher=CSIRO Publishing / Australian Biological Resources Study|isbn=0-643-05693-9}}</ref><!-- cites both previous sentences -->

The genus is classified in the subtribe [[Grevilleoideae|Embothriinae]] of the Proteaceae, along with the [[Alloxylon|tree waratahs (''Alloxylon'')]] from eastern Australia and New Caledonia, and ''[[Oreocallis]]'' and the [[Embothrium coccineum|Chilean firetree (''Embothrium coccineum'')]] from South America.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Johnson, L. A. S. |author2=Briggs, Barbara G. | year = 1975 | title = On the Proteaceae: the evolution and classification of a southern family | journal = Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society | volume = 70 | issue = 2 | pages = 83–182 | doi = 10.1111/j.1095-8339.1975.tb01644.x}}</ref><ref name="Weston 2006">{{cite journal |author1=Weston, Peter H. |author2=Barker, Nigel P. | year = 2006 | title = A new suprageneric classification of the Proteaceae, with an annotated checklist of genera | journal = [[Telopea (journal)|Telopea]] | volume = 11 | issue = 3 | pages = 314–44|doi=10.7751/telopea20065733 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Almost all these species have red terminal flowers, and hence the subtribe's origin and floral appearance must predate the splitting of [[Gondwana]] into Australia, Antarctica, and South America over 60 million years ago.<ref name=Nixon19>Nixon, p. 19.</ref>

Although no subspecies are recognised within ''Telopea speciosissima'' itself, geographical variations within its range have been noted. Forms toward the northern limits of its range have more prominently lobed leaves.<ref name=FoA/> A population from [[Waterfall, New South Wales|Waterfall]] has darker red, wider inflorescences,<ref name="Offord07"/> and a population at West Head in [[Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park]] has paler inflorescences.<ref name="Offord07"/> Leaf shape varies widely.<ref name="Offord07"/>

The [[common name]] ''waratah'' was first applied to this species before being generalised to other members of the genus ''Telopea'' and, to a lesser extent, ''Alloxylon''. ''Waratah'' is derived from the [[Eora]] Aboriginal people, the original inhabitants of the [[Sydney]] area.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/> The [[Tharawal people|Dharawal]] people of the Illawarra region knew it as {{lang|tbh|mooloone}},<ref name=Wesson05>{{cite web|url=http://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/resources/cultureheritage/illawarraAboriginalResourceUse.pdf|title=Murni Dhugang Jirrar: Living in the Illawarra|last=Wesson|first=Sue |date=August 2005|publisher=Department of Environment, Climate Change, and Water, State Government of New South Wales |page=7|access-date=22 February 2010}}</ref> and ''mewah'' is another aboriginal name. A former common name from around 1900 is "native tulip", possibly derived from ''Telopea''.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/><!-- cites prev 1.5 sentences -->

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Telopea speciosissima dist map.png|thumb|left|alt=Map of Australia showing a thin, nearly vertical continuous red blob on the lower right edge|Distribution of ''Telopea speciosissima'' (highlighted in red) within Australia]]
The species is found in [[New South Wales]] (Australia) from the [[Watagan Mountains]] southward to [[Ulladulla]], with a relatively widespread distribution in the [[Central Coast (New South Wales)|Central Coast]] region.<ref name=NSW/> It usually occurs as an [[understory]] shrub in open forest on sandy soils in areas with moderately high rainfall,<ref name=ANBG/> receiving on average around {{convert|1200|mm|in|abbr=on}} a year.<ref name=Nixon40>Nixon, p. 40.</ref> Dappled shade from [[Eucalyptus|eucalyptus (''Eucalyptus'')]] trees reduces sunlight by around 30%.<ref name=Nixon27/> Much of its range occurs in the [[Sydney Basin]], an area with one of the highest human populations and most intense development in Australia. The impact of [[habitat fragmentation]] and decreased fire interval (time between [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfires]]) on the gene pool of ''Telopea speciosissima'', which relies on [[outcrossing]], is unclear. Although largely protected within National Parks and conservation reserves in the Sydney area, most populations are small, numbering under 200 plants, and are often located near urban developments.<ref name="Offord07">{{cite journal|last=Offord|first=Cathy A.|year=2007|title=Floral- and leaf-character variation in waratah (''Telopea speciosissima'', family Proteaceae), with reference to conservation and horticultural improvement|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=55|issue=7|pages=684–91|doi=10.1071/BT06211 |bibcode=2007AuJB...55..684O }}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:Telopea speciosissima 5.jpg|right|thumb|Waratah in flower in bushland, regenerating from fire in recent years, dominant above slower-growing understory plants|alt=A shrub with a brilliant red flowerhead growing above grass among gum trees with blackened trunks from a bushfire]]
''Telopea speciosissima'' is a [[pyrogenic flowering|pyrogenic-flowering]] species, relying on post-fire flowering followed by production and dispersal of non-dormant seeds to take advantage of favourable growing conditions in the altered environment following a fire. Of the woody [[resprouter]] species of southeastern Australia, it is one of the slowest to produce seedlings after bushfires, taking at least two years.<ref name="denham02">{{cite journal|author1=Denham Andrew J. |author2=Auld, Tony D. |year=2002|title=Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=50|issue=5|pages=545–57|doi=10.1071/BT02009 |bibcode=2002AuJB...50..545D }}</ref><!-- cites para --> The species resprouts from a [[lignotuber]], a swollen woody base largely under the soil, that stores energy and nutrients as a resource for rapid growth of new shoots after a bushfire. Waratahs dominate the understorey around two years after a fire, but are later overtaken by the slower-growing [[Banksia|banksias (''Banksia'')]] and [[Acacia|wattles (''Acacia'')]]. Fire also serves to strip away diseases and pests.<ref name=Nixon256>Nixon, pp. 25–26.</ref> Flowering may be prolific at this time.<ref name="Parry59">{{cite journal|last=Parry|first=Percy J.|year=1959|title=How to grow waratahs|journal=Australian Plants|publisher=Surrey Beatty & Sons|location=Chipping Norton, NSW|volume=1|issue=1|page=2}}</ref>

[[image:Telopea speciosissima RNP.JPG|left|thumb|Fully mature flowerheads with opened florets, like this specimen from the [[Royal National Park]], attract many animals.|alt=A red dome-shaped flowerhead made up of hundreds of red flowers in late afternoon sun in bushland]]
The prominent position and striking colour of ''Telopea speciosissima'' and many of its relatives within the subtribe [[Embothriinae]] both in Australia and South America strongly suggest it is adapted to pollination by birds, and has been for over 60 million years.<ref name=Nixon19>Nixon, p. 19.</ref> Honeyeaters, in particular the [[New Holland honeyeater|New Holland honeyeater (''Phylidonyris novaehollandiae'')]]<ref name="affpoll"/> and the [[Crescent honeyeater|crescent honeyeater (''P. pyrrhopterus'')]],<ref name=Nixonp3>Nixon, plate 3.</ref> are frequent visitors. However, a field study conducted at Barren Grounds showed New Holland honeyeaters to carry relatively little pollen. The [[eastern pygmy possum|eastern pygmy possum (''Cercartetus nanus'')]] also forages among the flowerheads.<ref name="affpoll">{{cite web|url=http://www.aff.org.au/Whelan_waratah_final.pdf|title=Pollination in Waratah|author1=Whelan, Robert J.|author2=Goldingay, Ross L.|date=July 1989|publisher=Australian Flora Foundation|access-date=29 March 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091017223146/http://www.aff.org.au/Whelan_waratah_final.pdf|archive-date=17 October 2009}}</ref>

The New South Wales waratah had been considered to be [[Dichogamy|protandrous]] (that is, with male parts concluding sexual activity before female parts become receptive on the same plant),<ref name="Willis59"/> but analysis of the timing of pollen viability and stigma receptivity has shown significant overlaps.<ref name="Offord04">{{cite journal|last=Offord|first=Cathy A.|year=2004|title=An examination of the reproductive biology of ''Telopea speciosissima'' (Proteaceae) with emphasis on the role of protandry and self-pollination in fruit set.|journal=International Journal of Plant Sciences|volume=165|issue=1|pages=73–83|doi=10.1086/380745|s2cid=54511974}}</ref> The species has been shown to be self-incompatible, requiring [[Allogamy|cross-pollination]] with plants of other [[genotype]]s to reproduce successfully.<ref name="whel89">{{cite journal |title=Factors affecting fruit set in ''Telopea speciosissima'' (Proteaceae): The importance of pollen limitation |author1=Whelan, Robert J. |author2=Goldingay, Ross L. |year=1989|journal=Journal of Ecology|volume=77|issue=4 |pages=1123–34 |doi=10.2307/2260827|jstor=2260827 |bibcode=1989JEcol..77.1123W }}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Telopea comparison1 phils cropped.jpg|thumb|left|In cultivation, ''Telopea speciosissima'' on left next to larger more vigorous ''T''. 'Shady Lady' at right|alt=two green bushes growing in a garden bed next to a driveway]]

The New South Wales waratah was a popular garden plant at the beginning of the 20th century. It had been introduced early (1789) into the United Kingdom, and was reported flowering for the first time in 1809 at Springwell, the villa of one E. J. A. Woodford Esq. The [[Royal Horticultural Society]] awarded it an [[Award of Garden Merit|Award of Merit]] in 1914, and a First Class Certificate in 1922.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/>

Initially, waratahs were picked from the bushland for market, but by the early 20th century, a few [[plantsman|plantsmen]] grew concerned at the development of urban areas at the expense of bush, particularly areas noted for wildflowers. Percy Parry of Floralands in [[Kariong, New South Wales|Kariong]] developed the idea of "Preservation by Cultivation" and investigated the commercial cultivation of waratahs and other native plants. Meanwhile, the New South Wales Government was looking to curb flower and plant collecting from the wild, and considered prohibition in 1944, but after witnessing the ability of Parry to manage and develop cultivation, introduced compulsory licences for wildflower collecting the following year. With his wife Olive, Percy promoted and developed knowledge over fifty years and received the [[Order of Australia]] medal in 1981.<ref name=Nixon41>Nixon, p. 41.</ref> Following on from the Parrys were Howard Gay and Arch Dennis, who pioneered growing waratahs at Monbulk in the [[Dandenong Ranges]] in the 1940s, Sid Cadwell and Frank Stone, who did likewise in [[Dural, New South Wales|Dural]] and the Blue Mountains respectively.<ref name=Nixon42>Nixon, p. 42.</ref> The growing movement for cultivating and preserving native plants led to the establishment of the [[Australian Native Plants Society|Society for Growing Australian Plants]] in 1957,<ref name=Nixon42/> and the waratah was featured heavily in the first edition of its journal ''Australian Plants''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://asgap.org.au/payne.html|title=Vale – Bill Payne|last=Hockings|first=David|date=27 November 2005|work=Australian Native Plants Society website|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society |access-date=28 March 2010|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080720121056/http://asgap.org.au/payne.html |archive-date = 20 July 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Today, New South Wales waratahs are grown commercially in Australia north of Sydney and in the [[Dandenong Ranges]] near [[Melbourne]]. They are also grown commercially in [[New Zealand]] and in [[Israel]],<ref name=ANBG/> and also in [[Hawaii]], where they have been grown since 1961.<ref name=EJ10>{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake, Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Volume 9 – Sp-Z|year=2010 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=978-0-7344-0974-4|pages=200–03}}</ref> One major challenge in commercial production is that in any one location the flowering season is generally short (five weeks total, with only small numbers in the earliest and latest weeks). The season for cut flowers may be extended, however, by growing plants at different latitudes. The [[vase life]] of a cut waratah is 10 to 14 days, and cut flower waratahs can be revived somewhat by water.<ref name=Nixon25/>

Although they grow naturally on deep sandy soils, the species has proved adaptable to other deep, well-drained soils, especially where natural slopes assist drainage. Despite their natural occurrence in woodland, waratahs flower best in full sun, although they tolerate the dappled shade of eucalyptus.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991">{{cite book | last = Wrigley | first = John |author2=Fagg, Murray  | title = Banksias, Waratahs and Grevilleas | year = 1991 | publisher = Angus & Robertson | location = Sydney | isbn = 0-207-17277-3|pages = 538–41}}</ref> Heavy pruning after flowering reinvigorates the plants and promotes more profuse flowering in the next season.<ref name=ANBG/> Waratah blooms are highly susceptible to damage from wind, and benefit from some protection from [[prevailing winds]].<ref name=Nixon58>Nixon, p. 58.</ref> Waratah blooms attract birds to the garden.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/> The species is readily [[plant propagation|propagated]] from fresh [[seed]], but cultivars must be reproduced from cuttings to remain true-to-type.<ref name="Growing Waratahs">{{cite web|title=Growing waratahs|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/telopea/telopea.html|access-date=11 April 2010}}</ref>

Several species of fungi infect the roots of waratahs, causing significant plant morbidity or death. Typical symptoms include yellow leaves, wilting, blackening and dieback or part or all of the plant, or lack of [[cluster root|proteoid roots]].<ref name=Nixon56>Nixon, p. 56.</ref> The most common pathogen is the soil-borne [[oomycete|water mold]] ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'',<ref name=Nixon57>Nixon, p. 57.</ref> which appears to be more problematic in cultivated plants than in wild populations.<ref name=Woodford>{{cite news|author=Woodford, James|title=Waratah faces a fight to preserve its blooming life|work=The Age|url=http://www.smh.com.au/articles/2002/09/20/1032054962838.html|access-date=9 March 2010}}</ref> Mass plantings at the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney|Royal Botanic Gardens]] in Sydney and at [[Mount Annan]] planted before the [[2000 Summer Olympics]] were devastated by the disease.<ref name=Woodford/> ''[[Rhizoctonia solani]]'' can cause damping off or root rot,<ref name=Nixon57/> and is an uncommon pathogen. ''[[Cylindrocarpon scoparium]]'' and ''C. destructans'' (now ''[[Nectria radicicola]]'') are also uncommon causes of infection<ref>{{cite web|url=http://asgap.org.au/APOL5/mar97-4.html|title=Pests and Diseases of Australian Plants|author1=Summerell, Brett |author2=Steinke, Eve |year=1997|work=Australian Plants online|publisher=[[Australian Native Plants Society (Australia)]]|access-date=28 March 2010|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080728073546/http://asgap.org.au/APOL5/mar97-4.html |archive-date = 28 July 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> and result in decay of the crown of the plant.<ref name=Nixon57/> Although significant problems, fungi are less likely to be the cause of plant morbidity than poor drainage or soil conditions.<ref name=Nixon56/>

The larvae of the [[Acrocercops chionosema|Macadamia leafminer (''Acrocercops chionosema'')]], a [[moth]], burrow along and disfigure the waratah's leaves, and are mainly a problem in lowering the value of cut flower crops. More problematic is the larger caterpillar of another moth, the [[Xylorycta luteotactella|Macadamia twig girdler (''Xylorycta luteotactella'')]] which can burrow into and disfigure the developing flowerhead.<ref name=Nixon57/><!-- cites both sentences -->

=== Cultivars ===
[[File:Telopea light shade of pale 3 cropped.jpg|right|thumb|''Telopea'' 'Shade of Pale'|alt=A pale pink flowerhead made up of hundreds of pinkish flowers still a little greenish in the centre is nestled among its bracts and leaves.]]
A number of natural variants of ''Telopea speciosissima'' have been selected for cultivation as follows:
* '''''Telopea'' 'Brimstone Blush'''' is a shrub of smaller size than the species, reaching a metre (3 ft) tall, and was originally found growing on a property of Ben Richards in [[Oakdale, New South Wales|Oakdale]], southwest of Sydney. Flowering takes place in October. The flowerhead is globular with a pink crown and has 160 individual flowers, the styles of which are pink and white towards the ends. Three rows of whorled dark red bracts surround the flowerheads.<ref name=Nixon33>Nixon, p. 33.</ref>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Cardinal'''' is a form originally found on the property of Lucille Pope in Werombi, from where it was propagated and made available commercially. The original plant was a vigorous specimen reaching {{convert|3|by|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} and producing 100 to 120 flowerheads each year. It is named for its large dome-shaped cardinal red flowerheads, which bear 210 individual flowers and are surrounded by two rows of dark red bracts. These blooms have long vase life.<ref name=Nixon334>Nixon, pp. 33–34.</ref>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Corroboree'''', a form with longer styles, has compact inflorescences measuring {{convert|12|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and wide, and is a vigorous grower. It was selected for commercial propagation in 1974 by Nanette Cuming of [[Bittern, Victoria]], and registered with the [[Australian Cultivar Registration Authority]] in 1989. It is grown principally for the cut flower industry.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc457.html|title=Telopea 'Corroboree'|last=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|work=ACRA: Descriptions of Registered Cultivars|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=13 February 2010}}</ref>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Fire and Brimstone'''' is a vigorous form with large inflorescences selected by waratah grower and author Paul Nixon of [[Camden, New South Wales]]. It is a shrub which may reach 3–4 m tall and 2 m wide, with large leaves with more heavily toothed margins.<ref name=Wildside>{{cite book |last=Stewart |first=Angus |author-link= Angus Stewart|title=Gardening on the Wild Side|year=2001 |publisher=ABC Books |location=Sydney |isbn=0-7333-0791-4 |pages=132–38}}</ref> Each flowerhead is cone-shaped and has up to 240 florets. The stigmas are a light red and tipped with white. The bracts surrounding the flowerheads are relatively small, while the leaves are large and can reach {{convert|44|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in length.<ref name=Nixon34>Nixon, p. 34.</ref> The cultivar is thought to be [[Polyploidy|tetraploid]].<ref name=Wildside/> With a long vase life of 17 days, the cultivar is suitable for the cut flower industry.<ref name=Nixon34/>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Galaxy'''' has flowerheads with pinkish red tepals and white tips to the styles, surrounded by large bracts.<ref name=EJ10/>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Olympic Flame'''' is a form with prominent bracts around the flowerheads. It has large leaves with toothed margins and flowers in early spring. Also known as 'Sunburst', it arose as a seedling in a breeding program conducted by Cathy Offord, Peter Goodwin and Paul Nixon under the auspices of the [[University of Sydney]].<ref name=Wildside/>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Parry's Dream'''' was a [[chance seedling]] in the early 1970s. It gave rise to this cultivar, a vigorous plant with red-pink flowerheads which reach a diameter of {{convert|10|x|10|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} surrounded by pink bracts.<ref name=EJ10/>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Shade of Pale'''' is an unusual pale-pink flowered form of ''T. speciosissima''.<ref name=Wildside/> It is less vigorous than the parent plant. It was initially promoted as 'Light Shade of Pale' but there can only be three words in a registered cultivar name.
* '''''Telopea'' 'Sunflare'''' is an early-flowering form. It has large leaves with toothed margins and flowers in early spring. It also arose as a seedling in the same breeding program by the University of Sydney mentioned above.<ref name=Wildside/> Selected in 1981, it has red flowerheads with white-tipped styles which reach {{convert|9|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name=EJ10/>
[[Image:Wwaratah.jpg|thumb|right|''Telopea'' 'Wirrimbirra White'|alt=an overhead closeup view of a waratah flowerhead, this time a greenish white in colour]]
* '''''Telopea'' 'Wirrimbirra White'''' is a white form from Kangaloon near [[Robertson, New South Wales|Robertson]]. Aboriginal legends of white waratahs existed, and several had been encountered, but none had been previously preserved in horticulture. [[Joseph Maiden]] had previously found a white waratah near [[Kurrajong, New South Wales|Kurrajong]],<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/><!-- refs all para --> and others had been sighted near [[Narara, New South Wales|Narara]] on the Central Coast in 1919, and [[Colo Vale, New South Wales|Colo Vale]] in the 1950s. [[Horticulture|Horticulturalist]] Frank Stone reported one in his garden, possibly propagated from the latter plant.<ref name=Nixon38>Nixon, p. 38.</ref> 'Wirrimbirra White' was brought into cultivation in 1972 by cuttings from the original plant, which grew on [[Sydney Catchment Authority|water catchment]] property. It has pale greenish buds which open to a cream-white inflorescence. It is less vigorous than the parent species and vulnerable to [[Woodboring beetle|borers]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc322.html|title=Telopea 'Wirrimbirra White'|last=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|work=ACRA: Descriptions of Registered Cultivars|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=13 February 2010}}</ref> It is also highly vulnerable to the Macadamia twig girdler.<ref name=EJ10/>

In addition, a number of interspecific ''Telopea'' hybrids have also been produced. These have been bred or used as more frost- or shade-tolerant plants in cooler climates such as Canberra, Melbourne or elsewhere.

* '''''Telopea'' 'Braidwood Brilliant'''' is a frost-tolerant hybrid between a male ''T. speciosissima'' and female ''[[Telopea mongaensis|T. mongaensis]]''. Dr Boden of the Canberra Parks Administration began investigating this hybrid in 1962, and it was registered in 1975 by Richard Powell. It is a lignotuberous shrub to {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and has [[Leaf shape|oblanceolate]] leaves to {{convert|20|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long. The red blooms are {{convert|6|–|8|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter, intermediate in size between the parent species.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/> It has grown well in cooler climates such as Canberra.<ref name=Nixon32>Nixon, p. 32.</ref>
[[Image:Telopea 'Braidwood Brilliant'.jpg|thumb|''Telopea'' 'Braidwood Brilliant'|alt=a red flowerhead nestled among green foliage in a park setting]]
* '''''Telopea'' 'Canberry Coronet'''' is a cross between  ''T. speciosissima'' from [[Wentworth Falls]] in the [[Blue Mountains (Australia)|Blue Mountains]] and ''T. mongaensis'' intended for increased cold tolerance. It has red flowerheads to {{convert|6|–|8|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter. Reaching {{convert|3|–|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} high, it is a larger plant than 'Braidwood Brilliant'.<ref name=Wildside/> It was bred by Doug Verdon of the [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]] in Canberra.<ref name=Nixon33/>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Champagne'''' is a cultivar registered under Plant Breeders Rights (PBR) in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pericles.ipaustralia.gov.au/pbr_db/plant_detail.cfm?AID=6379143|title=Waratah (Telopea hybrid): Variety: 'Champagne'|year=2006|work=IP Australia: Plant Breeders Rights website|publisher=IP Australia, Commonwealth of Australia|access-date=18 December 2011}}</ref> Its creamy yellow flowerheads appear from October to December.<ref name=EJ10/> It is a three-way hybrid between ''T. speciosissima'', ''T. oreades'' and the yellow-flowered form of ''[[Telopea truncata|T. truncata]]''.
*  '''''Telopea'' 'Golden Globe'''' is a cultivar registered under PBR in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pericles.ipaustralia.gov.au/pbr_db/plant_detail.cfm?AID=6379141|title=Waratah (Telopea hybrid): Variety: 'Golden Globe'|year=2006|work=IP Australia: Plant Breeders Rights website|publisher=IP Australia, Commonwealth of Australia|access-date=18 December 2011}}</ref> Larger than 'Champagne', it is also a three-way hybrid between ''T. speciosissima'', ''T. oreades'' and the yellow-flowered form of ''T. truncata''. It has been propagated and sold as 'Shady Lady Yellow'. It was originally bred in the Dandenongs east of Melbourne.<ref name=EJ10/>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Shady Lady'''' is a larger shrub which may reach {{convert|5|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|2|or|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide. A hybrid of ''T. speciosissima'' and ''T. oreades'', it arose by chance in a Melbourne garden. The flowerheads are smaller and lack the bracts of the ''speciosissima'' parent. As its name suggests, it tolerates more shade.<ref name=Wildside/> It is vigorous and more reliable in [[Temperateness|temperate]] and [[Subtropics|subtropical]] areas, and grows in semi-shade or sun.<ref name=EJ10/> 'Shady Lady Crimson', 'Shady Lady Red' and 'Shady Lady Pink' are three selected commercially available colour forms.<ref name="Proteaflora">{{cite web|url=http://www.proteaflora.com.au/plant-search/other|title=Other Varieties|year=2010|publisher=Proteaflora|access-date=7 April 2010|location=Monbulk, Victoria|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110220153338/http://www.proteaflora.com.au/plant-search/other|archive-date=20 February 2011}}</ref>
* '''''Telopea'' 'Shady Lady White'''' is a white hybrid between ''T. speciosissima'' and ''T. oreades''.<ref name="Proteaflora"/>

== Symbolic and artistic references ==
The New South Wales waratah featured prominently in the folklore of the [[Darug people|Darug]] and [[Tharawal people]] in the Sydney basin and [[Gandangara people]] to the southwest.<ref name=Nice2000>Nice, p. 6.</ref> A [[dreamtime]] legend from the Eora tells of a female [[wonga pigeon]] searching for her husband who has been lost while out hunting. A hawk attacks and wounds her, and she hides in a waratah bush. Her husband calls and as she struggles in the bush her blood turns the white waratah blooms red.<ref>{{cite book|last=Mudrooroo|title=Aboriginal mythology: an A–Z spanning the history of aboriginal mythology from the earliest legends to the present day|publisher=[[HarperCollins]]|location=London|year=1994|page=142|isbn=1-85538-306-3}}</ref> A tale from the [[Burragorang Valley]] tells of a beautiful maiden named Krubi, who wore a red cloak of rock wallaby adorned with the feathers of the [[gang-gang cockatoo]]. She fell in love with a young warrior who did not return from battle. Grief-stricken, she died, and up from the ground grew the first waratah.<ref name=Nixon1516>Nixon, pp. 15–16.</ref> The Dharawal people regarded it as a totem, using it in ceremonies and timing ceremonies to its flowering.<ref name=Wesson05/>

The striking form of the New South Wales waratah became a popular [[motif (visual arts)|motif]] in [[Visual arts of Australia|Australian art]] in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century and was incorporated in [[Art Nouveau]] designs of the time. Matchboxes, paperweights and especially tins have been decorated with the flower. [[Arnott's Group|Arnott's]] often used the waratah as an alternative to their parrot logo on biscuit and cake tins from the early 1900s.<ref name=Nice54>Nice, p. 54.</ref> Shelleys soft drinks, established in 1893 in [[Broken Hill]], also displayed it on their label.<ref name=Nice54/> The French artist [[Lucien Henry]], who had settled in Sydney in 1879, was a strong proponent of a definitive Australian art style incorporating local flora, particularly the waratah.<ref name=Nice20>Nice, p. 20.</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Murray|first=Lisa|title=Lucien Henry|work=Dictionary of Sydney |url=http://trust.dictionaryofsydney.org/lucien-henry/|access-date=9 October 2013|date=9 October 2013}}</ref> His most famous surviving work is a [[triptych]] stained glass window of Oceania flanked by numerous waratahs overlooking the Centennial Hall in [[Sydney Town Hall]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Visions of a Republic: The Works of Lucien Henry|editor=McGee, Jude|publisher=Powerhouse Publishing |location=Sydney, New South Wales|year=2001|pages=96–97|isbn=1-86317-078-2}}</ref> In 1925, artist [[Margaret Preston]] produced a hand-coloured [[woodcut]] depicting waratahs.<ref>{{cite web|title=Margaret Preston|work=Floral Emblems of Australia|publisher=[[Australian National Botanic Gardens]]|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/emblems/preston.waratah.html|access-date=14 February 2010}}</ref> The species also appeared on an Australian 3 [[Shilling (Australian)|shilling]] stamp in 1959 designed by botanical illustrator Margaret Jones and a 30c stamp in 1968.<ref name=ANBG/>

The [[Sydney]] suburb of [[Telopea, New South Wales|Telopea]] takes its name from the Waratah, as does the [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]] suburb of [[Waratah]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Waratah: About the Area|publisher=The City of Newcastle|url=http://profile.id.com.au/newcastle/about?WebID=470|access-date=15 September 2013}}</ref> and the [[Super Rugby]] team, the Sydney-based [[New South Wales Waratahs]].

After [[Federation of Australia|Australian federation]] in 1901, the upsurge in nationalism led to the search for an official national floral emblem. The New South Wales waratah was considered alongside the wattle ''[[Acacia pycnantha]]'', and debate raged between proponents of the two flowers. The economist and botanist [[Richard Thomas Baker|Richard Baker]] proposed that the waratah's endemism to the Australian continent made it a better choice than the wattle, as well as the prominence of its flowers.<ref name=Nixon85>Nixon, p. 85.</ref> He was nicknamed the "Commander in Chief of the Waratah Armed Forces".<ref name=Nice30>Nice, p. 30.</ref> The South Australian ''Evening News'' also supported the bid, but to no avail.<ref name=Nixon85/>

Decades later, in 1962, ''Telopea speciosissima'' was proclaimed as the official floral emblem of New South Wales by the [[Governor of New South Wales]], [[Eric Woodward]], after being used informally for many years.<ref name=Nixon86>Nixon, p. 86.</ref> The species has also been adopted by others, including the [[New South Wales Waratahs]] rugby union team since the 1880s,<ref name=Nice54/> and the former department store [[Grace Bros]] in a stylised form for their logo in the 1980s.<ref name=Nice54/> Contemporary clothing designers [[Jenny Kee]] and [[Linda Jackson (designer)|Linda Jackson]] produced waratah-inspired fabric designs in the 1970s and 1980s during a resurgence of Australian motifs.<ref name=Nice56>Nice, p. 56.</ref><ref name=powerhouse>{{cite web|title=Influence of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander textiles on non-indigenous Australians|publisher=[[Powerhouse Museum]]|url=http://www.powerhousemuseum.com/hsc/paperbark/influence.htm|access-date=30 March 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100206152110/http://www.powerhousemuseum.com/hsc/paperbark/influence.htm|archive-date=6 February 2010}}</ref>

From 1956, the annual Waratah Festival was held in Sydney, run by the Sydney Committee. It took place from late October to early November, coinciding with the blooming of the waratahs. It was an important cultural event which included a parade, a popular art competition, beauty contests, exhibitions and performances.<ref>[http://www.theaustralian.com.au/news/arts/triumph-of-the-artificial/story-e6frg8n6-1111117049545 "Triumph of the Artificial"], ''[[The Australian]]'', 02-08-2008</ref> A highlight was the Lord Mayor's reception at the Sydney Town Hall for which the floral displays were made of hundreds of waratahs culled by Park Rangers from the national parks.

In 2009, the [[Premier of New South Wales]], [[Nathan Rees]], commissioned a state logo based on the floral emblem. The resultant logo design has been criticised as resembling a lotus rather than the New South Wales Waratah.<ref>{{cite news|last=Benson|first=Simon|date=16 July 2009|url=http://www.heraldsun.com.au/archive/news/nsw-premier-accidentally-replaces-waratah-with-lotus/story-e6frf7l6-1225750694164|title=NSW Premier accidentally replaces waratah with lotus |work=[[Herald Sun]] |location=Melbourne, Australia |publisher=[[News Corp Australia|News Limited]]|access-date=27 February 2015}}</ref>
